title: How to Connect a Reddit Integration in 2026, Step by Step
summary: A Reddit integration requires registering an app with Reddit's API using OAuth 2.0. You can call it from a script or a workflow tool like Activepieces.
body_markdown:
## Create a Reddit app and copy credentials


Open reddit.com/prefs/apps while logged in, create an app of the right type, and copy the client ID and secret it generates. Store both somewhere other than your repository before you do anything else.


Before it issues credentials for a new app, Reddit may also require you to request API access and describe your use case. Read its current terms first, because an unapproved app tends to fail with authorization errors that look like bugs in your code.


### Choose the right app type


Pick carefully, because Reddit offers three types and the choice decides how authentication works.


If the integration runs under your own account, such as a bot posting to a subreddit you moderate or a job pulling your saved posts, pick "script".


If other Reddit users will click through an authorization screen and grant your app access to their accounts, pick "web app".


For clients that can't keep a secret, such as a mobile app, there is the third type, "installed app". It has no secret to protect, so it's the wrong choice for anything running on a server.


A wrong pick here means rebuilding the auth flow later, so settle it before you touch the form.


### Fill in the Reddit app form fields


In Reddit's authorization screen, users see the name, so use one a user would recognize. The description and about URL are optional, but a real one helps if Reddit reviews your app.


Whatever the type, the redirect URI is required. A script app never uses it, so a localhost address is fine.


A web app must match it exactly, down to the trailing slash, or the authorization step fails with a redirect mismatch. Set your client's user agent string separately in code, because Reddit throttles generic ones harder.


### Find your Reddit client ID and secret


Once you create the app, Reddit lists it under "developed applications". The client ID is the short string directly beneath the app name and type, and it's easy to miss because it has no label.


The secret sits in a field labelled "secret". Mixing the two up is a common cause of an invalid-client error on the first request.


In a different place, the screenshot shows the same handoff. It's a dialog for enabling an OpenAI provider, with instructions to generate a key on OpenAI's site, a pre-filled Base URL, and an API Key field masked with asterisks.


The credential is created on the provider's side and the form only receives it. That's the point to take from it.


Reddit's ID and secret go into your client's configuration the same way. With both values stored, the next stage is making the first authenticated request.
